usage: Refers to the ravine and the cold stream running through it; a top summer escape spot
물 added; people say it to mean the cold water you dip your feet in
에서 marks the location of the activity
Most common adjective pairing in summer talk
examples: 여름엔 바다보다 계곡이 시원해서 좋아요.
In summer I like valleys better than the beach because they're cooler.
Common summer-trip opinion; 보다 compares the two
계곡에 발 담그니까 너무 시원하다.
Dipping my feet in the stream feels so refreshing.
발(을) 담그다 = dip feet in; very natural phrasing
주말에 계곡으로 물놀이 가기로 했어요.
We decided to go play in the water at a valley this weekend.
물놀이 = water play; 으로 marks destination
nuance: 계곡 means both the V-shaped ravine and, in everyday speech, the cold stream inside it. Koreans treat 계곡 as the classic budget summer getaway, so you'll hear it constantly from June to August. It's distinct from 강 (a wide river); a 계곡 is the narrow, rocky mountain version.
mistakes: Don't confuse 계곡 with 강 — 강 is a broad river, 계곡 is the rocky mountain stream/ravine.
Avoid spelling it 게곡; the correct vowel is ㅖ → 계곡.

usage: Plain noun; works for tiny and huge falls alike
수 added; emphasizes the falling water itself
떨어지다 (to fall) is the natural verb for water dropping
소리 = sound; often mentioned as the appeal
examples: 여기 폭포 소리 들으니까 마음이 편해져요.
Hearing the waterfall here makes me feel relaxed.
들으니까 = since/as I hear; ㄷ-irregular 듣다
비가 많이 와서 폭포 물줄기가 엄청 세요.
It rained a lot, so the waterfall's flow is really strong.
물줄기 = stream/jet of water; 세다 = to be strong
폭포 앞에서 사진 찍으면 시원해 보여요.
Photos taken in front of a waterfall look refreshing.
앞에서 marks the spot; 보이다 = to look/appear
nuance: 폭포 is a neutral, everyday word for any waterfall, from a small drop in a 계곡 to a famous tourist one. People often pair it with 소리 (sound) and 시원하다 (refreshing) when describing why they like it. It's a frequent hiking and travel-photo destination, so it comes up in casual weekend-plan talk.
mistakes: Don't write 포포 or 폭보; the word is 폭포 (ㄱ batchim then ㅍ).
폭포 is the structure/place; for the falling water itself you can add 수 → 폭포수, but for normal talk plain 폭포 is fine.

usage: Natural rock cave; also used figuratively for a cozy dark hideout
탐험 = exploration; common for tourist caves
안 = inside; 동굴 안은 시원해요 etc.
에 + 들어가다 for entering an enclosed space
examples: 동굴 안은 여름에도 엄청 시원해요.
Inside the cave it's really cool even in summer.
안은 = inside (topic); caves stay cold year-round
제주도에서 용암 동굴 구경했어요.
I checked out a lava cave in Jeju.
용암 = lava; Jeju's lava tubes are famous tourist spots
동굴이 어두워서 손전등이 필요해요.
The cave is dark, so you need a flashlight.
어둡다 → 어두워서; 손전등 = flashlight
nuance: 동굴 is the standard word for a natural cave, including Korea's famous limestone and Jeju lava caves that are popular day-trip spots. Locals also use it figuratively, as in 동굴 같은 방 (a cave-like room) for a dark cozy space. For tourism it's almost always paired with 구경하다 (to look around) or 탐험 (exploration).
mistakes: Use 동굴, not 굴 alone, in most travel contexts — plain 굴 also means 'oyster,' which causes confusion.
For entering, say 동굴에 들어가다 (에), not 동굴로 들어가다 unless you mean direction/route.

usage: Sheer rock face; also figurative for a dead end / crisis
끝 = edge/end; 절벽 끝에 서다 = stand at the edge
위 = top; views are described from 절벽 위
에서 marks the source of the fall
examples: 절벽 위에서 보는 바다 풍경이 진짜 멋있어요.
The ocean view from atop the cliff is really gorgeous.
풍경 = scenery; 위에서 = from on top
위험하니까 절벽 끝에 너무 가까이 가지 마세요.
It's dangerous, so don't go too close to the cliff edge.
가까이 = closely; safety warning at viewpoints
여기 해안 절벽이 사진 명소예요.
These coastal cliffs are a famous photo spot.
해안 = coast; 명소 = famous spot
nuance: 절벽 is a steep cliff or sheer rock face, common along Korea's coastlines and hiking ridges where signs warn you to stay back. It also has a strong figurative use — 절벽 끝에 몰리다 means to be pushed to the brink. In travel talk it usually appears with 해안 (coastal) or as a scenic 명소.
mistakes: Don't confuse 절벽 with 언덕 — 언덕 is a gentle hill, 절벽 is a vertical drop.
Spell it 절벽 (ㄹ batchim), not 절뼉 or 절벅.

usage: Coastal mud exposed at low tide; a west-coast specialty
체험 = hands-on experience; popular family activity
dig for clams in the mudflat
캐다 = to dig up; classic mudflat activity
드러나다 = to be revealed, at low tide
examples: 서해 갯벌에서 조개 캐는 체험을 했어요.
We did a clam-digging experience on the West Sea mudflats.
서해 = West Sea; signature west-coast activity
썰물 때 갯벌이 쫙 드러나요.
At low tide the mudflat gets fully exposed.
썰물 = low tide; 쫙 = mimetic for spreading wide
갯벌은 미끄러우니까 장화 신고 가세요.
Mudflats are slippery, so wear rubber boots.
미끄럽다 → 미끄러우니까; 장화 = rubber boots
nuance: 갯벌 is the muddy tidal flat exposed at low tide, a defining feature of Korea's West and South coasts and a popular hands-on 체험 for families and tourists. It's tied to tides, so you'll hear it with 썰물 (low tide) and activities like 조개 캐기 (clam digging). Korea's 갯벌 are even UNESCO-listed, so locals are proud of them.
mistakes: Pronounce/spell it 갯벌 (sai-siot ㅅ batchim), not 개벌 or 갯펄 in standard writing.
갯벌 only exists at low tide spots — don't use it for a regular sandy 해변 (beach).

usage: Coastal light tower; a very common seaside photo landmark
Ports often have a red and a white one as a pair
examples: 바닷가 등대 앞에서 사진 한 장 찍었어요.
I took a photo in front of the seaside lighthouse.
바닷가 = seaside; 한 장 = one (photo)
밤에 등대 불빛이 멀리까지 보여요.
At night the lighthouse beam is visible from far away.
멀리까지 = all the way far; 보이다 = be visible
빨간 등대 쪽으로 산책하면 노을이 예뻐요.
If you stroll toward the red lighthouse, the sunset is pretty.
쪽으로 = toward; 노을 = sunset glow
nuance: 등대 is a lighthouse, and in Korea harbor breakwaters famously have a 빨간 등대 (red) and 하얀 등대 (white) marking the channel. They're prime spots for seaside walks, sunset photos, and dates, so the word comes up in casual coastal-trip talk. It also carries a warm figurative sense of a guiding light.
mistakes: Don't mix up 등대 (lighthouse) with 등 (a lamp/light) or 등산 (hiking) — different words.
Say 등대 앞 / 등대 쪽 for location, not 등대에서 만나자 unless you literally mean meeting at its base.

usage: Where boats dock; think Busan, Sokcho, Tongyeong
도시 = city; Busan is the classic example
a ship comes into the harbor
a raw-fish place near the harbor
횟집 = sashimi restaurant; ports = fresh seafood
examples: 부산은 큰 항구 도시라서 회가 정말 신선해요.
Busan is a big port city, so the sashimi is really fresh.
회 = raw fish; 신선하다 = fresh
저녁에 항구에 배들이 하나둘 들어와요.
In the evening, ships come into the harbor one by one.
하나둘 = one by one; 들어오다
항구 앞에서 갓 잡은 생선을 팔아요.
They sell freshly caught fish right by the harbor.
갓 잡은 = freshly caught; 팔다 = to sell
nuance: 항구 is a harbor or port, strongly associated with Korea's coastal seafood cities like Busan, Sokcho, and Tongyeong. It implies the whole working waterfront — docks, boats, fish markets — so it's a common travel-destination word, especially for 회 (sashimi) trips. 항구 도시 (port city) is a set phrase locals use with pride.
mistakes: 항구 is the whole harbor; the specific docking pier is 부두 — keep the two distinct.
Don't confuse 항구 (harbor) with 공항 (airport), which reuses 항 but means something different.

usage: The built structure where ships tie up and load
여객선 = passenger ship; e.g. island ferries
examples: 부두를 따라 걸으면서 바다 구경했어요.
We looked at the sea while walking along the pier.
걸으면서 = while walking; ㄷ-irregular 걷다
섬에 가는 배는 저쪽 여객선 부두에서 타요.
You catch the boat to the island at that passenger pier over there.
여객선 부두 = ferry pier; 타다 = to board
부두에 큰 배가 정박해 있어요.
A big ship is docked at the wharf.
정박해 있다 = is (in a state of) being docked
nuance: 부두 is the specific built pier or wharf where boats tie up, as opposed to 항구, which is the whole harbor area around it. You'll need it most when catching island ferries (여객선 부두) or strolling a scenic waterfront. It's slightly more concrete and technical than 항구, but still everyday.
mistakes: Don't use 부두 and 항구 interchangeably — 부두 is the pier structure, 항구 is the entire harbor.
Spell it 부두, not 부뚜 (부뚜막 is a stove ledge, a totally different word).

usage: Wide open grassy or farmland field in the countryside
넓다 → 넓은; the most natural pairing
펼쳐지다 = to spread out, of scenery
examples: 기차 창밖으로 넓은 들판이 펼쳐졌어요.
Wide open fields stretched out beyond the train window.
창밖 = outside the window; 펼쳐지다
가을이 되면 들판이 노랗게 변해요.
When autumn comes, the fields turn yellow.
노랗게 = yellowly; rice paddies ripening
들판에서 자전거 타니까 진짜 시원했어요.
Riding a bike across the field felt really refreshing.
자전거 타다 = ride a bike; 시원하다
nuance: 들판 is a wide open field or plain — farmland, grassland, the scenery rolling past a countryside train window. It carries a calm, spacious, rural feeling and often shows up in descriptions of 가을 (autumn) when rice fields turn gold. It's broader and more scenic than 밭 (a cultivated crop field).
mistakes: Don't confuse 들판 (open plain/scenery) with 밭 (a specific cultivated crop plot).
Spell it 들판 (ㄹ batchim + 판), not 들빤 or 들반.

usage: A small rise, much smaller than a 산 (mountain)
위 = top; cafes and views are 언덕 위에 있다
오르다 = to go up; also 언덕을 올라가다
가파르다 = steep; common for tiring uphill streets
examples: 언덕 위에 전망 좋은 카페가 하나 있어요.
There's a cafe with a great view on top of the hill.
전망 = view; 하나 있다 = there's one
집까지 가는 길이 언덕이라서 좀 힘들어요.
The way home is uphill, so it's a bit tiring.
언덕이라서 = because it's a slope; 힘들다
봄에는 언덕에 꽃이 잔뜩 펴요.
In spring the hill blooms with tons of flowers.
잔뜩 = a whole lot; 피다 → 펴요
nuance: 언덕 is a hill or gentle slope — far smaller than a 산 (mountain) but enough to make you huff on the walk home. In Korean cities, hillside neighborhoods and 언덕 위 카페 (hilltop cafes) with views are a real thing. It also describes the tiring incline of a street, as in 우리 집은 언덕에 있어요.
mistakes: Don't call a real mountain an 언덕 — use 산 for mountains, 언덕 for small hills/slopes.
Spell it 언덕 (ㄴ batchim + 덕), not 언떡 or 언덬.

usage: An individual mountain peak; a range has several
산 prefixed; very common combined form
오르다 = to ascend; 정상까지 오르다 similar
examples: 설악산은 봉우리가 여러 개라서 풍경이 멋져요.
Seoraksan has several peaks, so the scenery is spectacular.
여러 개 = several; 풍경 = scenery
저 멀리 눈 덮인 봉우리가 보여요.
You can see a snow-covered peak far in the distance.
눈 덮인 = snow-covered; 보이다
가장 높은 봉우리까지 두 시간쯤 걸려요.
It takes about two hours to reach the highest peak.
가장 높은 = the highest; 걸리다 = to take (time)
nuance: 봉우리 is a single mountain peak or summit, and a ridge or range is made up of several 봉우리. Hikers use it constantly when describing famous mountains like 설악산 or 지리산. The combined form 산봉우리 is also very common, and it pairs naturally with 정상 (the very top) in trail talk.
mistakes: 봉우리 is one peak; the highest point/top is 정상 — don't treat them as identical.
Spell it 봉우리, not 봉오리 (봉오리 means a flower bud, a different word).

usage: The sandy shore area; slightly more 'beach' than plain 바다
산책 = stroll; very common seaside activity
가 (edge) added; 해변가 카페 = beachside cafe
examples: 여름에 강릉 해변으로 놀러 갔어요.
In summer I went to play at Gangneung's beach.
강릉 = Gangneung; 놀러 가다 = go to have fun
해변을 따라 걸으니까 노을이 너무 예뻤어요.
Walking along the beach, the sunset was so pretty.
따라 = along; 노을 = sunset glow
해변에 사람이 별로 없어서 조용했어요.
There weren't many people on the beach, so it was quiet.
별로 없다 = not many; 조용하다 = quiet
nuance: 해변 specifically means the sandy beach/shore, whereas 바다 is the sea itself — so you swim in the 바다 but lay your towel on the 해변. East-coast spots like Gangneung and Sokcho are the go-to 해변 destinations. It pairs naturally with 산책 (stroll) and 노을 (sunset) for that classic seaside outing.
mistakes: Don't swap 해변 (the shore) for 바다 (the sea) — 해변에서 수영하다 sounds off; you swim 바다에서.
해변 and 해수욕장 overlap, but 해수욕장 specifically means a designated swimming beach with facilities.
